tldr: The authors propose RoboTwin-Phys to systematically benchmark variations in physical parameters—such as mass and friction—that were previously overlooked in robot manipulation, revealing that modern foundation models drop significantly in performance under changing physical conditions despite being robust to visual changes.
hero_caption: An overview of the 13 physical factors introduced in RoboTwin-Phys. Spanning five categories—object properties, contact, damping, work environment, and camera placement—it covers the physical variability encountered in the real world.
overview:
Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) that incorporate world models have driven significant progress toward general-purpose robot manipulation skills. Simulator-based evaluations have also scaled up, making it common practice to randomize object appearances, textures, lighting, camera viewpoints, and scene layouts. However, there has been a critical blind spot: the underlying physical parameters—such as mass, friction, and center-of-mass positions—have remained fixed in most benchmarks.

In the real world, the mass and center of mass of the same mug change if it is filled with liquid, and an older table or gripper will show changes in friction and joint damping. Whether models that are resilient to visual changes can also tolerate such variations in physical properties had never been systematically verified. To address this, the authors extended the dual-arm evaluation platform RoboTwin-2.0 to build "RoboTwin-Phys," an evaluation benchmark that continuously varies 13 physical attributes across episodes.

Furthermore, they curated over 5,000 feasible expert demonstrations labeled with ground-truth physical parameters and evaluated representative WAMs and VLAs. The results showed that models handling visual and layout randomization with ease suffered sharp drops in success rates as soon as physical conditions were varied. In other words, current models do not truly understand or adapt to physical contacts and dynamics. This work introduces "physical robustness" as a vital new evaluation dimension needed for robot foundation models to operate reliably in the real world.
contributions: Built "RoboTwin-Phys," a new robot manipulation benchmark that continuously varies 13 physical attributes, including object mass, friction, and joint damping.
Introduced a framework that adjusts feasible parameter bounds per task and verifies the existence of solutions using an expert planner in advance to prevent unrealistic parameter breakdown.
Released a high-quality dataset of over 5,000 expert demonstrations labeled with 13-dimensional ground-truth physical parameters.
Comprehensively evaluated representative WAMs (Fast-WAM, Motus, FACT) and VLAs (π0.5, Galaxea-VLA), demonstrating a substantial "physical robustness gap" that is independent of visual variations.

sections.heading: Visual Changes Aren't Enough: The Hidden Blind Spot in Physical Parameters
sections.summary: While existing robot manipulation benchmarks have diversified visuals and scene layouts, the underlying physical parameters have stayed fixed. As a result, robustness to unavoidable real-world variations like mass and friction could not be measured, and ground-truth physical data for training remained scarce.
sections.details:
Recently, VLAs that directly output actions from vision and language, as well as WAMs that act while predicting environment transitions, have shown impressive results. Alongside this progress, large-scale simulation environments for dual-arm robots like RoboTwin-2.0 have enabled reproducible training and fair model comparisons.

However, current benchmarks carry a major blind spot: physical-condition diversity. Modern simulators have pushed robots' visual adaptability by heavily randomizing object textures, lighting, camera positions, and initial poses (domain randomization). Meanwhile, physical properties such as object mass, friction coefficients, center of mass (CoM), and joint viscous damping have typically remained fixed at default baseline values.

In reality, filling a container with liquid shifts both its mass and its center of gravity, and surface wear alters friction. These are decisive factors directly governing the success of contact-rich manipulation. Despite this, prior studies have only tested individual factors on a small scale, lacking a standardized evaluation protocol, large-scale data collected across diverse physical conditions, and ground-truth physical labels for model training.

To solve this problem, this work introduces "RoboTwin-Phys" based on 50 tasks from RoboTwin-2.0, continuously sampling 13 physical attributes on an episode basis. This exposes whether models can truly withstand changes in the physical world beyond mere visual alterations.

sections.heading: How the 13 Physical Factors Are Designed and Realistically Sampled
sections.summary: RoboTwin-Phys independently samples 13 physical attributes per episode guided by three principles: physical validity, continuous diversity, and composability. It incorporates task-specific bounds to prevent extreme-value breakdowns and an expert-based pre-feasibility check.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Benchmark Design Principles
Rather than arbitrarily perturbing parameters with random noise, RoboTwin-Phys is built around three core principles:
- Physical validity: Sampled conditions must reflect operating environments that could realistically occur in the real world rather than absurd simulation configurations.
- Continuous diversity: Values are varied continuously across a meaningful range rather than selected from a few discrete cases.
- Composability: Physical condition shifts are treated as an independent evaluation axis that can be assessed either separately from or simultaneously with traditional visual and layout randomization.

At the beginning of each episode, 13 physical attributes are sampled and kept constant throughout the episode. This reproduces complex environmental variations where multiple physical factors interact simultaneously.

### 2.2 Sampling Physical Conditions
The 13 targeted physical factors span five categories: object properties (mass, center of mass, scale), contact properties (friction coefficient, restitution coefficient), damping properties (object joints, robot arm joints, gripper damping), work environment (table tilt, table height, external disturbance forces), and camera placement (distance, angle). Because values are tied to the episode seed, experiments remain fully reproducible.

### 2.3 Task-Specific Physical Parameter Tuning
Applying a single uniform range across all tasks causes issues. For instance, in a task handling an elongated hammer, setting the CoM offset range too wide could push the center of mass outside the hammer's physical mesh—creating an impossible setting that works numerically but makes no sense in reality. The authors addressed this by empirically tuning individual allowable ranges for 9 physically sensitive tasks, eliminating unreasonable edge-case failures.

### 2.4 Pre-Feasibility Verification
If a generated environment is physically impossible to complete in the first place, it cannot fairly evaluate a policy. Therefore, an automated expert planner is run beforehand on each sampled environment. Any episode the expert cannot solve is filtered out of the evaluation pool, ensuring that any subsequent failure by a model is genuinely due to its lack of physical adaptability.

sections.heading: Over 5,000 Expert Demonstrations Labeled with Ground-Truth Physics
sections.summary: To turn physical conditions into explicit learning targets rather than hidden simulation variables, the authors constructed a dataset of over 5,000 demonstrations. Every episode is accompanied by 13-dimensional ground-truth physical parameters as metadata.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Dataset Construction
Alongside the benchmark, the authors released the "RoboTwin-Phys Training Set v1" for model training. This dataset contains over 5,000 expert episodes sampled from the defined physical condition distributions. Mirroring the benchmark design, task-specific safety bounds are applied, and all data is collected in valid environments where success has been verified. Standard visual and layout randomizations can also be layered on top.

### 3.2 Providing Ground-Truth Physical Parameters
The key feature of this dataset is that each demonstration is annotated with the ground-truth 13-dimensional physical parameters active during that episode's execution.

In conventional robot learning, physical parameters have remained buried as invisible internal simulator states. With this dataset, however, several promising avenues of research become readily accessible:
- Training models that estimate physical attributes (like mass or friction) from visual observations or past action histories
- Condition-aware representation learning that explicitly acquires physical conditions as latent embeddings
- Training adaptive policies that take physical parameters as input to fine-tune their behavior

Data structures are fully compatible with the official RoboTwin format, allowing seamless integration into existing WAM and VLA training pipelines.

sections.heading: Experiments: What Happens to State-of-the-Art Models When Physics Changes?
sections.summary: Three WAMs and two VLAs were evaluated across three setups: Clean, Official Random (visual and layout), and Physical Random. All models suffered a steep drop in success rates to 31–44% under Physical Random, revealing a universal challenge across architectures.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Evaluated Models
Experiments compared model resilience across three environment protocols:
- Clean: A baseline environment where all randomization is disabled.
- Official Random: An environment applying only conventional visual and layout randomization, keeping physical parameters fixed.
- Physical Random: An environment where the 13 physical attributes of RoboTwin-Phys are sampled on top of conventional randomization.

Five models were evaluated: three representative World-Action Models (WAMs)—Fast-WAM, Motus, and FACT—and two representative Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)—π0.5 and Galaxea-VLA (G0.5).

### 4.2 Overall Results: A Substantial Robustness Gap
The experimental results (Table 1) were striking. When moving from Clean to Official Random, performance drops for WAM models were negligible (a 0.10 point drop for Fast-WAM, 1.64 points for Motus, and 1.80 points for FACT; for VLAs, Galaxea-VLA dropped by 0.90 points and π0.5 by 5.98 points). These models proved remarkably robust to changes in appearance and layout.

However, entering the Physical Random environment completely changed the picture. Success rates plummeted across the board: Fast-WAM fell to 44.24%, Motus to 39.60%, FACT to 39.14%, π0.5 to 31.60%, and Galaxea-VLA to 37.82%. Despite differences in architecture and training methods, all five models experienced similar heavy performance degradations. This fact demonstrates that vulnerability to physical changes is not a bug unique to a particular model, but a fundamental challenge shared across current robot learning.

### 4.3 Task-Level Trend Analysis
Analyzing individual success rates across all 50 tasks revealed common strengths and weaknesses across models. For example, tasks like hammering a block (beat_block_hammer), moving a stapler (move_stapler_pad), picking varied bottles (pick_diverse_bottles), and putting bottles in a dustbin (put_bottles_dustbin) suffered severe drops across all models. Conversely, tasks such as grasping a roller or shaking a bottle maintained relatively high robustness.

### 4.4 Discussion
What the low-scoring tasks share is a heavy reliance on contact dynamics, object stability, center-of-mass shifts, and multi-link kinematics. These tasks cannot be solved simply by moving a gripper to a target pose; they require immediate adjustments in force and approach based on the object's mass and slipperiness—demands under which current models consistently break down.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: Toward Robots That Adapt to the Physical World
sections.summary: RoboTwin-Phys is the first systematic benchmark measuring robots' physical adaptability. The experiments highlight the physical vulnerabilities of current foundation models, pointing toward future models that explicitly perceive, reason about, and adapt to physical conditions.
sections.details:
This paper proposed RoboTwin-Phys, introducing physical-condition diversity as an evaluation dimension for robot manipulation. By continuously varying 13 physical attributes within plausible ranges and compiling over 5,000 ground-truth-labeled expert demonstrations, it serves not only as an evaluation suite but also as a training testbed for physics-adaptive models.

Evaluations of representative WAMs and VLAs clearly demonstrated that conventional robustness to visual randomization does not guarantee physical robustness at all. Variations in physical conditions uncover a new dimension of failure modes that remained invisible under existing benchmark protocols.

The authors anticipate that RoboTwin-Phys will serve as a foundational stepping stone for embodied AI research, paving the way toward next-generation robot control models capable of explicitly sensing, reasoning over, and adapting to the physical world.

sections.heading: Appendix: Specific Parameter Values and Task-Specific Edge Cases
sections.summary: The appendix details the global sampling ranges for the 13 physical attributes, custom configurations for 9 tasks designed to prevent geometric inconsistencies, and the file structure of the released dataset.
sections.details:
### Global Ranges of Physical Attributes and Task-Specific Tuning
Appendices A and B define the specific numerical ranges configured in the simulator. In the global configuration, realistic variation ranges are specified for each of the 13 attributes, including object mass multipliers, friction coefficients, restitution coefficients, center-of-mass offsets, joint damping, table tilt and height, and camera displacement and field of view.

However, directly applying global ranges leads to failures on certain tasks. For example, setting large CoM offsets on elongated objects places the center of mass outside the mesh. Custom upper and lower bounds were therefore redefined for affected tasks (9 tasks, including beat_block_hammer). This completely eliminates artificial failures stemming from physically unrealistic setups.

### Data Format and Structure
The dataset structure described in Appendix C is organized as follows:
- data/: HDF5 files containing robot actions, internal states, and camera visual streams
- video/: MP4 videos recording execution runs
- phys_meta/: JSON files recording the exact ground-truth values for the 13 attributes sampled in each episode

Additionally, Appendix D provides success rates across all 50 tasks for each model, enabling in-depth analysis of which contact-rich motions cause particular models to fail.

takeaways: Robustness to visual variations and robustness to physical property variations are entirely separate capabilities, making physics-based evaluation essential.
Even cutting-edge WAMs (Fast-WAM, Motus, FACT) and VLAs (π0.5, Galaxea-VLA) see their success rates plummet to the 30–40% range when mass and friction change.
Tasks relying heavily on contact and center-of-mass balance (such as striking, placing, and precision grasping) are extremely vulnerable to physical variations.
The ground-truth-annotated dataset in RoboTwin-Phys can accelerate research into physical attribute estimators and physics-conditioned adaptive policies.
limitations: Evaluations remain confined to a simulation environment (RoboTwin-2.0), leaving untested how effectively policies trained for physical adaptation transfer to physical hardware (Sim-to-Real).
The evaluated models were architected without physical parameters as inputs; direct comparisons against methods that explicitly take physics as input remain for future work.
Manual adjustments were required on 9 tasks to keep sampling bounds plausible, creating manual tuning overhead as task numbers scale up.
